message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Pricing Proposal, Weekend Rate Restructure (Harbourside Hotel)

The case for raising the weekend rate is reasonable. Harbourside sits £20–£35 below its competitive set and sold out on 31 Saturdays. Its competitive position and occupancy figures support a rise, and a rise may well be right.

The proposal's three main supports don't hold, however:

- **The price-sensitivity "test" is seasonality.**
- **The £204,000 uses the wrong room count** and applies the rise to bookings that won't pay it.
- **The two-night minimum works against the hotel's largest Saturday segment.**

So £204,000 is not a floor. Even if volumes hold, it is closer to a ceiling.

## 1. The June-to-July "test" measures the season, not the price

The rate rose by £10 in the last week of June, and July occupancy rose from 81% to 89%. Section 2 explains why July is always stronger: "July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays." The occupancy rise in July is exactly what the season predicts, with or without a price change.

The comparison has two further weaknesses:

- **June was partly treated.** The new rate applied to the last week of June, so June is not a clean "before" month.
- **One month can't separate price from season.** A meaningful test compares July–December 2025 with the same months of 2024, when the old rate applied. Better still, compare booking pace before and after the change.

As it stands, the data are consistent with weekend guests being price-sensitive, insensitive or anything in between. They don't support "not price sensitive." The idea that the rise "reinforced our positioning" has no evidence behind it at all.

## 2. The value-for-money score doesn't support it either

A value score of 8.4, the best in the set, is partly a consequence of being the cheapest. Raising prices to the level of the cheapest competitor is likely to lower it.

The score is also collected from guests who chose to book at £145, so it can't show how guests who would be lost at £165 would respond. It suggests some room to raise prices, but it doesn't show how much.

## 3. The revenue estimate is overstated

| Step | Annual figure |
|---|---|
| As stated: 124 rooms × 104 nights × 79% × £20 | £204,000 |
| **Using 112 rooms** (Section 2's figure) | **£184,000** |
| Less wedding and group blocks at contracted rates (about 19% of weekend room-nights; see below) | about £149,000 |
| Ex-VAT, if BAR is quoted VAT-inclusive (standard in UK) | about £124,000 |

On the third row: wedding blocks are 38% of Saturday room bookings, which is about 19% of all weekend nights. Section 6 confirms that contracted group rates will be honoured, so these bookings don't move with BAR. Any other non-BAR business, such as packages, member rates or corporate weekend stays, reduces the figure further.

OTA commission on bookings through online agents also takes a share of the extra £20 on those bookings.

Together with the first year's partial effect (bookings already taken for June onward were made at £145), a defensible estimate on unchanged volume is roughly **£110,000–£125,000 a year**, not "at least £204,000."

## 4. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business

Section 4 reports that wedding guests account for about 38% of Saturday bookings and typically stay one night, arriving Saturday and leaving Sunday. A blanket two-night minimum on every stay including a Saturday works directly against that segment:

- **Future wedding blocks** are presumably negotiated as groups, but individual wedding guests booking at BAR will be forced into a second night or elsewhere. Other hotels near Quayside Hall will gladly take them, and the relationship with the venue is at stake.
- **On sell-out Saturdays** (31 in 2025), a minimum stay can make sense, because single-night demand exceeds supply and turning some away costs little.
- **On the other 21 Saturdays**, it turns away single-night guests who would have filled empty rooms. That is lost revenue, not extra revenue.

So the minimum stay doesn't only add unquantified revenue: it can reduce revenue. "£204,000 is a floor" assumes its effect can only be positive. Standard revenue-management practice is to apply minimum stays selectively on high-demand dates, which here means excluding or coordinating around wedding dates.

## 5. Monitoring

- **Use revenue per available room, not occupancy.** At £165, weekend room revenue stays above the 2025 level unless occupancy falls below about **69%**, roughly 10 points down. A five-point occupancy trigger may therefore fire while the change is still paying off. Before it can fire, though, the comparison has to account for wedding and festival dates differing from 2025.
- **Define the action.** "We will review the rate" should state what would happen, such as rolling back on unconstrained dates or lifting the minimum stay on specific weekends.
- **Lead with pace.** The weekly pick-up comparison is the right early indicator, more so than monthly occupancy.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Room count.** 112 or 124? The Section 5 figure needs correcting, or Section 2 does if the hotel has expanded.
- **Positioning.** £165 matches the cheapest competitor. That is a positioning change from cheapest to joint-cheapest and is worth stating openly.
- **Notice period.** Two weeks' notice to OTAs is short, and existing June–August bookings will remain at £145. The first year's gain will be smaller.

## Recommendation

- **The rate rise is defensible on competitive grounds.** Restate the expected gain as about £110,000–£125,000 a year, net of contracted business and VAT, and treat it as a target that depends on volume holding, not a floor.
- **Replace the "test" with a real one.** Compare July–December 2025 with 2024, or phase the rise, starting on high-demand dates.
- **Apply the minimum stay selectively** on dates expected to sell out, and agree an approach with Quayside Hall for wedding weekends.
- **Monitor revenue per available room against booking pace**, with a defined response.
